Lorsqu’on est asiatique, il peut être di: When you are Asian, it can be hard to talk about mental health. Misunderstanding and taboos surround the subject. However, the racism the community has faced throughout the pandemic has brought the issue to light. The mental health of Asian people is affected by a variety of realities, such as adoption, immigration and adapting to the host society.
Viet Tran, India Deblois, Julie Tran, Ki: Viet Tran, India Deblois, Julie Tran and Kimura Byol at the press conference of the Coalition asiatique pour une relève émancipatrice (CARE).
India Deblois et Kimura Byol sont deux p: India Deblois and Kimura Byol are two people of Asian origin who were adopted. Although they grew up on two different continents and are decades apart in age, both have experienced abandonment, inner conflict and a sense of alienation from the Asian community.
« J’ai eu beaucoup de difficulté avec l’: “I struggled a lot with abandonment. I often wondered why I was alive,” India Deblois confides. Adopted along with her sister by a white family in the Beauce region, she felt out of place and confused about her identity. “I couldn’t connect to a Chinese identity, because I didn’t know anything about that culture,” explains the student. And it is a conflict she still lives with today. When she hears her colleagues talk about their Asian traditions at the Korean restaurant where she works, she feels left out. “We’re not Asian enough to be understood by other Asians, and we’re not white enough for white people,” she sums up. Before moving to Montréal in the middle of the pandemic, Ms. Deblois studied at Université Laval.
Elle éprouvait des difficultés à l’école: She struggled at school because she felt alone, without an Asian community. It was this painful experience that led her to see a psychologist for two years. “During my sessions, I told him that I didn’t feel comfortable, that my friends didn’t understand my interests, that I had no role model in life,” she explains. The prospect of moving to the metropolis, where a large Asian community exists, seemed to her a way to fill that void. As soon as she arrived, the young woman began looking for people who looked like her. She enrolled in the Korean language and Asian studies program at Université de Montréal and found a job at a Korean restaurant.
« M’impliquer dans des activités liées a: “Getting involved in activities connected to Asian cultures, meeting people, taking part in the march against anti-Asian racism – all of these things helped me heal,” she says. For his part, Kimura Byol uses his artistic work as a balm. “When I get insulted, I turn it into art. Working artistically lets me calm down and deconstruct the attack,” says the artist confidently. “I realize it’s not my fault, but the fault of others and of a society that accepts this kind of negative behaviour.”
Pour en arriver à ce genre de détachemen: Reaching that kind of detachment took Kimura a great deal of effort. Born in Korea and raised by a white family in Belgium in the 1970s, the artist often heard hurtful remarks from his own adoptive parents. “They said they weren’t racist toward Asians, but they openly said they were toward others. They insulted Asians, but claimed we weren’t Asian because we were adopted,” Kimura recounts. The artist lived under pressure to adopt the same cultural norms as his parents. Kimura was also worried about his future. When he was young, there weren’t many Asian role models in Belgium.
À son souvenir, les seuls qu’il y avait: As he remembers it, the only ones there were amounted to “the actress in the music video for David Bowie’s song China Girl and hypersexualized images of Asian women.” During his adolescence, the lack of political power of adopted people and having to depend on his parents outraged him deeply. Kimura even thought about taking his own life. “As an adopted person, I had no Asian adults around me. So adult life was such an abstract concept for me,” the artist says. Today, Kimura fights to make the voices of adopted people heard. His works, which deal with his various identities and life experiences, have been exhibited across Canada as well as in Europe and Asia.
Pour certains, c’est une immigration dif: For some, a difficult immigration journey is at the root of their suffering. Every day, Jin Xing, a mortgage advisor at CIBC, waits patiently for her permanent residence. And every evening after another day without news, she goes to bed depressed and unable to fall asleep. “All my days are grey. Seeing the people around me – my friends, my colleagues, people on my social media – with status hurts me enormously,” she confides in a voice thick with emotion. Things haven’t always been this bleak.
Il y a cinq ans, Mme Xing et son mari ar: Five years ago, Ms. Xing and her husband arrived from China full of hope. He, then in his fifties, hoped to go back to school and change his life after a military career of more than 20 years in the Chinese army. Ms. Xing, who was returning from a three-year stay in Ghana where she had worked, already had a command of French and was eager to start a new career. For two years, she took training to prepare for her current job, and she passed her French exam with flying colours. The couple’s dreams quickly turned into nightmares under the pressure of the immigration process. After submitting their application for permanent residence, the couple received nothing but silence from the Canadian government in response. “We haven’t received anything, no letters, no results. We’re still waiting,” she says in despair. Despite sustained efforts, her husband has still not managed to get a work permit. The stress of having to support her family on her salary alone and the endless wait have worn down the mortgage advisor’s spirit.
« Je ne suis pas motivée, car je n’ai pa: “I’m not motivated, because I don’t feel like I have a future. Every time I listen to the news and hear that the Canadian government is welcoming more newcomers, I get depressed,” she says. “I’ve been here five years, I’m anxious, I’m getting no results.” Ms. Xing has run into several obstacles while trying to get psychological help. When you lack time and money, it is extremely hard to access care. She also worries about her husband, who also needs care and still doesn’t have his health insurance card. “Me, I just received mine this year. Before that, I had to pay for all my health care out of pocket. Finding a professional who speaks Mandarin is also difficult – my husband needs one, he speaks neither French nor English,” she says. It is also hard to get an appointment with a psychologist. Ms. Xing waited several months for a spot to open up, but eventually gave up on the idea.
Ces expériences l’ont rendue extrêmement: These experiences have made her extremely cynical. She arrived in Canada with big plans, and now she no longer even knows whether it is worth staying. She hopes reforms to the immigration and health systems will be put in place. “I want the government to tell us the exact waiting times for getting status or a work permit,” she demands. “I also want mental health services that are adapted to our culture and accessible to people without status. But I have little hope that it will ever happen.”
Face aux traumatismes et à l’isolement d: Faced with trauma and the isolation of many elders, isolation that was made worse by lockdown, the community felt the need to come together. It gathered on October 2 in Montréal to discuss mental health. In the room, you could see the spirit of camaraderie of a community reuniting after a long year marked by the pandemic and anti-Asian racism. At the press conference organized by the Coalition asiatique pour une relève émancipatrice (CARE), the organization launched four video clips on mental health and the Asian community.
Le quotidien de Julie Tran, l’une des tr: The daily life of Julie Tran, one of the three administrators of the Groupe d’entraide contre le racisme envers les Asiatiques, is punctuated by stories of the discrimination, hardships and challenges that members of the group face. “When Asian people go through these experiences, they tend to deny their mental health impact. When people started sharing their experiences, many said it was the first time they had felt a sense of solidarity. It gives them some relief in terms of their mental health,” she explains. Ms. Tran believes the community can serve as an instrument of healing. “Young people have started sitting down with their parents and grandparents to talk about mental health and racism,” says the University of Ottawa social work graduate.
« Ça permet aux générations précédentes: “It helps older generations understand that activism isn’t dangerous. Often, our parents live with their own trauma, and it’s hard for them to bring up these subjects,” she says. Ms. Tran hopes these efforts to improve the mental health of community members will continue in the future. She stresses the importance of funding community organizations and the need for an institution to counter anti-Asian racism. “I have often shown up in activist spaces where there was no other Asian person. In those spaces, we are just racialized people who get lumped in with other realities,” she says, expressing her frustration. “Our realities are made invisible.
Il faut une personne asiatique aux table: There needs to be an Asian person at the tables where decisions are made.” Making Asian realities visible in the public sphere is Viet Tran’s mission. It is the mandate that this trained psychiatrist has given himself as editor-in-chief of Sticky Rice. Launched last year, the magazine covers the realities of Canadians of Asian origin. “Being able to recognize yourself in the words, the images, the creations of the publication can be restorative for your mental health,” he believes, adding that it can help continue the healing process and spark new reflections. In the course of his professional consultations, Dr. Tran has noticed that his Asian patients had distinct mental health experiences.
« Plus on se sent proche de notre pays a: “The closer we feel to our Asian country of origin, the more our mental health depends on our interpersonal relationships,” he tells us. According to him, in Asian societies, which are rather collectivist, an individual’s well-being depends on their role within their family or among their colleagues. “When Asian people come to see me, they talk to me about their failures in their roles as a parent, a sibling or a professional,” the psychiatrist says. “My non-Asian patients, who have more individualistic values, will rather talk about their individual failures, like not having gotten their dream job.” The psychiatrist is optimistic about the growing number of mental health professionals of Asian origin who understand the realities of their community. He is nevertheless aware of the formidable obstacle that language represents. For first-generation immigrants who speak only their language of origin, access to care is still very limited.
Le Dr Tran sait aussi que recevoir des s: Dr. Tran also knows that receiving mental health services is still taboo in the Asian community. He suggests other options for those looking for alternatives, including cultural community centres and spiritual places. He cites as an example the Chùa Quan Âm pagoda, which his family attends. “These places can be beneficial for recharging. Many of us find that community ties are a source of support and that we don’t find that in individual therapy,” he concludes.
